DEVORE-04-KDC-DEFAULTDOMAINSUPPORTEDENCTYPES Disable RC4 at the domain level on domain controllers

HIGHUnknownnot confirmed by this scan

Found: not confirmed by this scanTarget: exactly 56

Why this is unknown — this is not a pass

Group Policy doesn't show this setting's value, so the scan can't confirm it either way. Use the check below to settle it.

  • No GPO sets the KDC default. Devore's instruction for this control is to create the value on the domain controllers, which leaves no GPO trace, so absence from Group Policy is not evidence that RC4 remains available domain-wide - this scan reads Group Policy and cannot see the value either way.
  • Reported as 'unknown', not as a failure. This control's documented remediation is a direct registry write on the domain controllers, which leaves no trace in Group Policy at all, so the key appearing in no GPO is NOT evidence that the value is unset. This scan reads Group Policy and not the machines, so it cannot see the live value either way and issues no verdict. Check it on each domain controller with: reg query "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\services\KDC" /v "DefaultDomainSupportedEncTypes"
  • 1 GPO(s) could not be read and were not searched for this key: CN={33333333-3333-3333-3333-333333333333},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=test,DC=local

Remediation

Set DefaultDomainSupportedEncTypes to 0x38 on domain controllers, as the final lock-in after per-account (service account) AES remediation. Devore's instruction is to create the value directly on the DCs; delivering it as a GPO registry preference is equivalent and is the only form this scan can verify.

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 56. The catalog gives no audit step for this one. That doesn't make it safe to apply everywhere at once, so read the warnings below.

Before enforcing, check: 4768 Ticket Encryption Type = RC4 identifies the accounts and devices that still depend on RC4.

Watch out for:

  • The post warns that big-bang use is 'too aggressive for most' — treat this as the final step, after per-account remediation, not the opening move.
  • NOT GPO-DELIVERED: the documented remediation creates the value on the domain controllers, so absence from Group Policy proves nothing. Where no GPO sets the key the finding is 'unknown', not 'fail', and carries the reg query command to check it on the DCs. Where a GPO does set it - as on the verified domain, at 0x38 by registry preference - it is scored normally.

DEVORE-03-LDAP-CLIENT-SIGNING LDAP client signing requirement

MEDIUMUnknownnot confirmed by this scan

Found: not confirmed by this scanTarget: at least 2 (step 1: at least 1)

Why this is unknown

1 of 3 GPO(s) could not be read, so it is unproven that no GPO sets this key; the documented Windows default was not applied

Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LDAP client signing requirements' = 'Require signing' (the OS already gives you 'Negotiate signing' without a GPO, so setting Negotiate explicitly buys documentation, not hardening).

How to roll it out safely

Step 1: set it to 1 first (audit mode). This makes the setting visible on every machine without blocking anything yet.

Step 2: only then set it to 2. Don't skip step 1: enforcing before every device and service account is ready can cause sign-in failures and account lockouts.

The catalog doesn't say what to check before enforcing. Treat that as a catalog gap, and pilot it first.

Watch out for:

  • Windows already defaults to Negotiate (1); Windows SASL binds will not break when DCs start requiring signing unless a GPO overrode that default with 0.
  • OS DEFAULT, NOT ENFORCEMENT: where no GPO sets this key the finding rests on the documented default and is marked 'source: os-default'. That is a pass at the Negotiate step, not evidence that anything prevents a future GPO from setting 0.

DEVORE-03-LDAP-DIAG-LOGGING Enable LDAP Interface diagnostic logging (find unsigned binds)

INFORMATIONALUnknownnot confirmed by this scan

Found: not confirmed by this scanTarget: at least 2

Why this is unknown — this is not a pass

Group Policy doesn't show this setting's value, so the scan can't confirm it either way. Use the check below to settle it.

  • No GPO sets the diagnostic level. Devore's own instruction for this control is a direct registry write on the domain controllers, which leaves no GPO trace, so absence from Group Policy is not evidence that the level is 0 and the 2889 evidence is not being produced - this scan reads Group Policy and cannot see the level either way.
  • Reported as 'unknown', not as a failure. This control's documented remediation is a direct registry write on the domain controllers, which leaves no trace in Group Policy at all, so the key appearing in no GPO is NOT evidence that the value is unset. This scan reads Group Policy and not the machines, so it cannot see the live value either way and issues no verdict. Check it on each domain controller with: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Diagnostics" /v "16 LDAP Interface Events"
  • 1 GPO(s) could not be read and were not searched for this key: CN={33333333-3333-3333-3333-333333333333},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=test,DC=local

Remediation

Set the '16 LDAP Interface Events' diagnostic level to 2 or higher on domain controllers while collecting unsigned-bind evidence. Devore's instruction is a direct registry write on each DC: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Diagnostics" /v "16 LDAP Interface Events" /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f. Delivering the same value through a GPO registry preference is equivalent and is the only form this scan can verify.

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 2. The catalog gives no audit step for this one. That doesn't make it safe to apply everywhere at once, so read the warnings below.

Watch out for:

  • NOT GPO-DELIVERED: the documented remediation writes the registry directly on each domain controller, so this scan cannot confirm the level from Group Policy. Where no GPO sets the key the finding is 'unknown', not 'fail', and carries the reg query command to check it on the DCs.
  • An audit enabler, not a hardening endpoint: it generates 2889 (client IP, account, binding type), 2887 (daily unsigned volume) and 2888 (rejected after enforcement).
  • Leaving it raised permanently is noisy; it is normally raised for the audit window only.
  • Levels run 0-5 with increasing verbosity (Microsoft, 'AD and LDS diagnostic event logging'; default 0), so a level above 2 satisfies this control - it logs strictly more, including the 2889 events. The floor is 2, not the exact value 2.

DEVORE-01-NTLM-LMCOMPATIBILITYLEVEL Enforce NTLMv2 via LAN Manager authentication level

HIGHFailstage: not startedCONFLICT

Found: 1 in Evil <script>alert("xss")</script> & 'quoted' GPO; 5 in Sample Override GPOTarget: at least 5 (step 1: at least 3)

Conflict — enforced-override

2 GPOs set this key to different values and at least one is linked with enforcement (Sample Override GPO = 5), so the other settings are likely overridden. Precedence is not resolved here — verify with RSoP / gpresult before trusting any single value.

GPOValueRollout stepDelivered byEnforced link

Sample Override GPO
CN={22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=test,DC=local		5enforcedsecurity template (policy)yes

Precedence is unresolved. Confirm the effective value with gpresult /h or the Group Policy Results (RSoP) wizard against a representative machine before changing or trusting any of these settings.

Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level'. Bring all clients and member servers to 'Send NTLMv2 response only' (3) first, then raise domain controllers to 'Refuse LM & NTLM' (5).

How to roll it out safely

Step 1: set it to 3 first (audit mode). This makes the setting visible on every machine without blocking anything yet.

Step 2: only then set it to 5. Don't skip step 1: enforcing before every device and service account is ready can cause sign-in failures and account lockouts.

Before enforcing, check: 4624 with LmPackageName='NTLM V1' on members and endpoints. 4776 on DCs does not record the NTLM version. Exclude ANONYMOUS LOGON.

Watch out for:

  • PHASED: do not set domain controllers to 5 until every device is at 3+. At 5 a DC treats NTLMv1 as bad-password attempts, which causes lockouts (the author saw 46 failed logons from one NTLMv1 SMB connection).
  • 0-3 govern what the client requests; 4-5 govern what the server/DC accepts.
  • TATTOOING: the key lives outside HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies, so setting it and later returning the policy to 'Not Defined' leaves the value behind; it must be cleared per device.
  • Credential Guard ignores this setting and disables NTLMv1 on its own. No reboot required.

DEVORE-06-SMB-CLIENT-SIGNING-ALWAYS SMB client require signing (always)

HIGHFailstage: not startedno GPO sets this

Found: no GPO sets thisTarget: exactly 1

Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled, on endpoints and member servers as well as domain controllers.

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 1. The catalog gives no audit step for this one. That doesn't make it safe to apply everywhere at once, so read the warnings below.

Watch out for:

  • NOT THE LEGACY SETTING: 'Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)' / EnableSecuritySignature is a different, weaker setting that applies to SMBv1 only — Microsoft states it is ignored by SMB2 and later ('does nothing unless you're using SMB1') and recommends against using it. A GPO setting EnableSecuritySignature = 1 does NOT satisfy this control, and this control does not look at that value name.
  • '(always)' applies to all SMB versions and terminates sessions where the peer cannot sign.
  • Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require SMB signing by default, so an unset key is not necessarily unsigned traffic on those builds — but it is also not enforced by policy, which is what this control asserts.

Where the value comes fromMicrosoft, 'Overview of Server Message Block signing in Windows' — 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)' | Registry key: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManWorkstation\Parameters | Registry value: RequireSecuritySignature | Data Type: REG_DWORD | Data: 0 (disable), 1 (enable): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/smb-signing-overview — policy semantics ('always' = required) in Microsoft, 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/microsoft-network-client-digitally-sign-communications-always CASING IS VERBATIM: the page writes the registry path with 'LanMan' (capital M), which is what is quoted here. Elsewhere on the same page the *Administrative Templates* auditing policy paths are written 'Lanman Server' / 'Lanman Workstation' — a different thing from the registry key, and not a reason to re-case this quote. Real GPOs spell the service names inconsistently too; normalize_registry_key handles that, so the catalog keeps the source's casing rather than the wire's.

DEVORE-08-NTLM-AUDIT-INCOMING Audit incoming NTLM traffic

MEDIUMFailstage: not startedno GPO sets this

Found: no GPO sets thisTarget: at least 1

Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic' = 'Enable auditing for domain accounts' (or 'for all accounts').

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 1. The catalog gives no audit step for this one. That doesn't make it safe to apply everywhere at once, so read the warnings below.

Watch out for:

  • FLOOR, NOT LEVEL: >= 1 means some auditing is enabled; 0 fails as 'auditing configured off'. Microsoft documents the option set (Disable / domain accounts / all accounts) but not the numerics, so the domain-vs-all-accounts distinction is reported in the evidence rather than scored — read the found value if you need to know which level is set.
  • INFERRED, NOT CITED: that the off option ('Disable') is stored as the numeric 0, and every other option at 1 or above, is not printed by Microsoft — it is an inference from Microsoft's statement that the unset policy behaves as 'Disable'. See value_source for the inference and why a floor (and only a floor) is safe to rest on it; the exact level is never scored.
  • TRAP: third-party write-ups conflate the Audit* and Restrict* value mappings and will tell you a value of 2 here means 'deny all'. It does not — Microsoft is explicit that this audit policy 'doesn't actually block any traffic'. Blocking is DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-INCOMING, which stays unscored for want of a sourced numeric.

WHY THIS IS HELD WHILE DEVORE-08-NTLM-AUDIT-OUTGOING SCORES ON THE SAME VALUE NAME: the two controls need different amounts of the mapping. A *floor* needs only two facts — that the permissive option is stored as 0, and that every other option is >= 1 — and both follow from Microsoft's statement that an unset policy behaves as 'Allow all' (an absent REG_DWORD reads as 0). It never has to know which number is 'Audit all' and which is 'Deny all', and it claims nothing about them. An *exact* target has no such luxury: 'Deny all' is one specific numeric out of three, no floor can express it ('gte 1' is equally satisfied by 'Audit all'), and guessing it would report an audit-only domain as blocking outgoing NTLM. So the audit control asserts exactly what the inference supports and stops there, while this control cannot be stated at all without the numeric Microsoft does not print. registry_key is left null so that no part of the pipeline can present this control as checked. Source the deny numeric from a Microsoft Security Baseline or CIS Benchmark to activate it.

This scan doesn't work out which GPO wins when several set the same setting (policy precedence, RSoP). It reports every GPO that sets it, with its link path, and flags disagreements as conflicts. For a conflict, check the effective value with gpresult /h before acting.

Catalog notes
  • Check types in this release: gpo-security-template (GptTmpl.inf [Registry Values]) and gpo-registry-pol (Registry.pol). The catalog's directory-state controls (DEVORE-02 SMBv1, DEVORE-04 msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes, DEVORE-07 least privilege, DEVORE-08 Protected Users) have no evaluator yet and are deliberately absent rather than present-and-unevaluatable; they arrive with their own engine.
  • registry_key is the full path including the value name (its last component). For gpo-registry-pol the evaluator splits the last component off to match Registry.pol's separate key/value fields; for gpo-security-template the whole path is one [Registry Values] key.
  • Rollout is phased, not binary: interim_expected is the audit/negotiate step and final_expected the enforced step, so a domain correctly mid-rollout reports rollout_state 'audit' and result 'pass', not a failure.
  • os_default records the value Windows uses when no GPO sets the key, and only where a Microsoft document states it. Such a finding is evaluated against the default and marked 'source: os-default', so an assumed value is never mistaken for an enforced one. It is deliberately absent where there is no default to cite — LdapEnforceChannelBinding, for one, has no such key by default (channel binding is off), which is precisely why configuring it matters. Two limitations are deliberate. A finding resting on a default is capped at rollout_state 'audit', because 'enforced' means Group Policy holds the value and nothing enforces a default. And os_default is a single value, so a default that depends on the machine's role cannot be expressed: DEVORE-06-SMB-SERVER-SIGNING-ALWAYS is 'Enabled' by Microsoft's table for domain controllers but 'Disabled' for member servers and clients. Making that expressible would need the evaluator to know which machines a GPO lands on, which a SYSVOL/GPO scan cannot see at all — so those controls carry no default and say why in missing_note, rather than asserting one role's default over the whole domain.
